name: omms-memory
description: Search and save OMMS project memory. Use before you debug or investigate a problem, when the user refers to earlier work ("we fixed this before", "last time", "remember", "did we"), and before a decision about project conventions. Use after the user makes a decision, you fix a bug, or the user states a preference.

# OMMS project memory

OMMS keeps memories for each project: earlier fixes, decisions, and conventions. At the start of a session OMMS adds the closest matches to the context. That list is partial. Search the full store before you work out an answer again.

## How to call OMMS

- If your tool list has a `memory` tool, use it. Pi and OpenCode call it `memory`. Claude Code with the OMMS plugin calls it `mcp__omms__memory`.
- If no `memory` tool is listed, run the `om-memory-system memory` command with the Bash tool from the project directory. Each command prints one JSON document. A result with `"success": false` has an `error` field.

## Using OMMS in Claude Code

- Recall arrives as added context. The user sees it as `▸ ● memory [mode=…]` rows at the top of your reply. The context holds the closest matches only.
- When `mcp__omms__memory` is listed, call it. Do not run the command through Bash.
- The tool refuses the `import`, `export`, `migrate` and `list-shards` modes. Tell the user to run them with `om-memory-system memory` in a terminal.
- With hand-written hooks or an older plugin, no `memory` tool is listed. Then run `om-memory-system memory` through Bash.
- Each injected memory shows its id. When the user asks you to remove that memory, pass the id to `forget`.
- Memory spaces keep separate stores. The context line `Active memory space: <name>` names the one in use. Use `space` mode to list or switch spaces when the user asks. Deleting a space and moving memories between spaces are only possible in the web app. Export and import of a space run in the web app or with `om-memory-system space` in a terminal; the tool refuses them.
- Capture runs after each reply in the background. Do not save the same turn again, unless it holds a decision, a fix or a preference that the user asked you to keep.

## When to search

Search first:

- before you debug or investigate a problem;
- when the user refers to earlier work, for example "we fixed this before", "last time", "remember", or "did we";
- before a decision about project conventions, tools, or structure.

Use `recall` instead when the user quotes a memorisation ID or asks what was planned or memorised, for example "what were we gonna do with the release notes" or "what did I memorise". Recall searches memorisations only. When the user asks for the memorisation labelled X, use `recall` with `tags: "X"`, not `search`. Use `search` for other questions about earlier work.

```text
memory({ mode: "recall", query: "<ms- ID or topic>" })
memory({ mode: "recall", tags: "<label1,label2>" })
```

With the command:

```bash
om-memory-system memory recall "<ms- ID or topic>"
om-memory-system memory recall --tags "<label1,label2>"
```

A labelled recall returns only memorisations that carry every label. Add a query to narrow by text as well.

With the `memory` tool:

```text
memory({ mode: "search", query: "<keywords>" })
```

With the command:

```bash
om-memory-system memory search "<query>"
```

- Use technical keywords, for example `"database choice"` or `"webhook retry policy"`.
- If the first search finds nothing, try two or three other keyword sets: the error text, the file name, the tool name.
- If the project search finds nothing, search every project: `scope: "all-projects"` with the tool, or `--scope all-projects` with the command.
- Each result has `id`, `content`, `similarity` (0 to 100), and `type` when the memory has one. Add a limit (`limit: N` or `--limit N`) to get fewer results.

## When to save

After the user makes a decision, after you fix a bug, or after the user states a preference, save one short memory.

With the `memory` tool:

```text
memory({ mode: "add", content: "<one or two sentences>", type: "<type>", tags: "<tag1,tag2>" })
```

With the command:

```bash
om-memory-system memory add --content "<one or two sentences>" --type <type> --tags "<tag1,tag2>"
```

- Write the content so that it makes sense without the conversation. Name the files, tools, and reasons.
- Save a personal working preference that applies to all projects with mode `profile` (`om-memory-system memory profile --content "<preference>"`).

Types:

| Type            | Use for                                   |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `decision`      | A choice and its reason                   |
| `bug-fix`       | A bug, its cause, and the fix             |
| `feature`       | A feature that was added                  |
| `refactor`      | A change of structure with no new feature |
| `configuration` | A setting, environment, or build change   |
| `analysis`      | A finding from an investigation           |
| `discussion`    | A conclusion from a discussion            |
| `other`         | Anything else                             |

## Modes

| Mode          | Options                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `search`      | query, limit, scope                                                                                                                          |
| `memorise`    | content, or topic, done, doing and next for a session snapshot; tags (labels)                                                                |
| `recall`      | query (a memorisation ID or topic), tags (labels), limit                                                                                     |
| `add`         | content, type, tags                                                                                                                          |
| `list`        | limit, scope                                                                                                                                 |
| `forget`      | the memory id                                                                                                                                |
| `space`       | action (`list`, `status`, `create`, `use`, `archive`, `unarchive`, `preview`, `copy`, `link`, `unlink`), name, to, since, until, project, in |
| `profile`     | no options to show the profile; content to save a preference                                                                                 |
| `list-shards` | none                                                                                                                                         |
| `migrate`     | the old path or hash, dry run                                                                                                                |
| `export`      | the output file                                                                                                                              |
| `import`      | the input file, dry run                                                                                                                      |
| `help`        | none                                                                                                                                         |

The command takes each option as a flag, for example `--query`, `--limit`, `--scope`, `--id`, and `--directory <path>` for a different project. Run `om-memory-system memory --help` for the full list.

Space options: `to` names the target space of a preview or copy; `since` and `until` are inclusive ISO 8601 dates; `project` is the project tag; `in` names the space that owns a link (the active space by default). A recalled memory from a linked space carries `space="<name>"`. `forget` and `edit` refuse such a memory and name its space.

## Safety

- Never store secrets: API keys, tokens, passwords, or private keys.
- OMMS removes text inside `<private>...</private>` tags before storage. Content that is fully private is not stored.
- Do not use `forget` unless the user asks you to remove a memory.

name: omms-remember
description: Save a short session snapshot in OMMS from the current context, then report its ID. Use when the user asks to memorise, remember, or save this session, its progress, or its next steps for a later session. Do not read session history or transcript files.
---

# OMMS session snapshot

Save a short snapshot of the current session in OMMS. Use plain British English and short sentences. A fresh agent can then recall the work without the chat history.

Do not ask the user questions. Do not write a handover file or a paste-ready prompt.

## Write the snapshot

1. Use only what you already hold in the current context. Do not read session history, transcripts, logs, or prior conversation exports.
2. You may run cheap read-only git commands to confirm the current branch and head commit. Do not inspect diffs, logs, or history to rebuild the session.
3. Fill these fields from the current context:
   - `topic`: the project, change, or subject.
   - `done`: completed work, with task IDs or file names where useful.
   - `doing`: work in progress. Leave it out when nothing is in progress.
   - `next`: the next actions and any gate that blocks them.
4. Omit empty fields. Keep the whole snapshot short enough to stay under the configured memorisation size cap. OMMS never shortens it for you.
5. Never store secrets: API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, or other credentials. Do not copy raw secret-bearing output into any field.

## Save with memorise

If your tool list has a `memory` tool, use it. Pi and OpenCode call it `memory`. Claude Code with the OMMS plugin calls it `mcp__omms__memory`.

```text
memory({
  mode: "memorise",
  topic: "<project, change, or subject>",
  done: "<completed work>",
  doing: "<work in progress>",
  next: "<next actions and gates>"
})
```

Use `mode: "memorise"` with only the fields that have content. Do not add a transcript or a long conversation summary.

When the user supplies text to memorise, save that text with `content` instead of inventing snapshot fields:

```text
memory({ mode: "memorise", content: "<text the user names>" })
```

Send `content` or the snapshot fields in one call, never both. The tool refuses a call with both. When the user's text already has done, doing and next parts, put them in the snapshot fields.

## Labels

Every memorisation can carry labels. Labels are the `tags` argument, a comma-separated list.

- When the user names labels, for example "memorise this, label it release, wip", pass every label the user names in `tags`, exactly as written. Never drop, reword or merge a user label.
- Add 1 to 3 labels of your own that describe the topic. Keep them short and lower-case. Do not repeat a label the user gave.
- When the user names no labels, still add 1 to 3 labels of your own.
- Do not put `memorisation` in `tags`. OMMS adds that fixed tag itself.

```text
memory({
  mode: "memorise",
  topic: "<topic>",
  next: "<next actions>",
  tags: "<user labels as written>,<your 1 to 3 labels>"
})
```

With the command, add `--tags "<labels>"`:

```bash
om-memory-system memory memorise --topic "<topic>" --next "<next>" --tags "release,wip,auth"
```

Use the `om-memory-system memory` command only when no `memory` tool is listed. Run it from the project directory:

```bash
om-memory-system memory memorise --topic "<topic>" --done "<done>" --doing "<doing>" --next "<next>"
```

For text the user supplies:

```bash
om-memory-system memory memorise "<text>"
```

Each command prints one JSON document. A result with `"success": false` has an `error` field. If the snapshot exceeds the size cap, shorten the fields and retry. Report the error if the save still fails.

## Report and recall

Tell the user the returned `ms-` ID. Say they can recall the snapshot later by quoting that ID, by asking about its topic, or by asking for a label.

To recall by label, use `recall` with `tags`. Only a memorisation that carries every label matches. Add `query` to narrow by text as well. With `tags` and no `query`, recall returns the newest matches. Use this when the user asks for "the memorisation labelled X".

```text
memory({ mode: "recall", tags: "<label1,label2>" })
```

With the command:

```bash
om-memory-system memory recall --tags "<label1,label2>"
```

Use mode `recall` when the user quotes a memorisation ID or asks what was planned or memorised, for example "what were we gonna do with the release notes" or "what did I memorise". Use mode `search` for other questions about earlier work.

```text
memory({ mode: "recall", query: "<ms- ID or topic>" })
```

With the command:

```bash
om-memory-system memory recall "<ms- ID or topic>"
```

## Invocation names

- Claude Code: `/omms:omms-remember`
- Pi: `/skill:omms-remember`
- OpenCode: `/omms-remember`

# OMMS: Opinionated Modular Memory System [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/om-memory-system.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/om-memory-system) [![npm downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/om-memory-system.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/om-memory-system) [![MIT licence](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/om-memory-system.svg)](LICENSE.md) OMMS gives AI coding agents long-term project memory. It captures technical work, recalls relevant notes in later sessions and learns your working preferences. One shared engine serves **OpenCode**, **Pi** and **Claude Code**, so each host can retrieve memories captured by the others in the same project. Memories are stored locally, by default in `~/.omms/data`. Embeddings run locally by default; the first use downloads a search model. Capture and profile learning make additional model calls that can send conversation content to your chosen provider and incur costs. Remote embeddings are optional. OMMS removes text inside `` tags before storage. See [Configuration](docs/configuration.md) for model choices and privacy controls. ## Set up Use Node.js **22.14 or later** for the terminal command and Claude Code hooks. OMMS supports OpenCode v2, Claude Code and the [Pi coding agent](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent). > Automatic history import is enabled by default and makes model calls. > To disable it before your first session, set `"autoBackfill": false` in > `~/.config/omms/omms.jsonc`. See [Automatic import](docs/web-ui-memory.md#automatic-import). ### OpenCode Add the package to `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`. Keep your existing settings. On Windows, use `%USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode\opencode.json`. ```json { "plugins": ["om-memory-system"] } ``` Or run: ```bash opencode plugin add om-memory-system ``` Restart OpenCode. The [OpenCode guide](docs/opencode-adapter.md#installation) covers plugin management and its additional `cli.json` configuration. ### Pi ```bash pi install npm:om-memory-system ``` Restart Pi. See the [Pi guide](docs/pi-adapter.md). ### Claude Code Install the OMMS plugin using the [Claude Code guide](docs/claude-code-adapter.md#installation). Capture and profile learning require a configured external API; retrieval and manual memory operations remain available without it. A global npm install is optional. ### Model and web app With no model settings, OpenCode and Pi use the session model. You can choose a host model or configure an external API under **Settings**. Claude Code uses only the external API. See [Choosing the model](docs/configuration.md#choosing-the-model) for the selection order and credentials. Start a host session, then open [http://127.0.0.1:4747](http://127.0.0.1:4747). Each host starts the shared web app when needed, unless it is disabled. Browse captured notes on **Project memories**, or ask your agent to search memory for an earlier decision. Each host adds only the memories that match your prompt. An optional setting also adds matching memories to the first message of a new session. See [Host differences](docs/using-memory.md#host-differences). ### Terminal command (optional) A global install puts `om-memory-system` on your `PATH`: ```bash npm install -g om-memory-system om-memory-system --version ``` See the [CLI reference](docs/cli.md) for manual memory operations and history imports. ## Inside OMMS These screenshots use synthetic examples and configuration. All visible prompts, code snippets and outcomes are made up for the demonstration. ### Project memories Browse captured notes alongside example user input and technical outcomes. ![Project memories with synthetic English prompts, code and outcomes](.github/screenshots/project-memories.png) ### Memory Pick a host card (Pi, OpenCode or Claude Code) to see its import status, sessions and folders that need a map. The Shared card holds profile learning, memory limits and other settings that apply to every host. The cards also warn you when memories cannot be saved. ![Memory page showing the Pi host view with synthetic import status](.github/screenshots/memory.png) ### Memory spaces Keep separate stores for separate lines of work. The Spaces item in the web app sidebar opens a page with one card for each space. Switching a space applies to every host. Memories can be copied or moved between spaces, exported to a shareable file and imported into a new space, and a space can read the spaces it links. See [Memory spaces](docs/memory-spaces.md). ### Memorisations Save an exact note on purpose and fetch it later by ID, such as `ms-4k7q2p`, or by a close description. A memorisation stays out of automatic recall and cleanup, and the Memorisation page lists, labels, filters and deletes them. See [Memorise and recall](docs/using-memory.md#memorise-and-recall). ### Settings Choose models and manage access. Diagnostics show capture outcomes and component health. ![Settings page with synthetic model configuration](.github/screenshots/settings.png) ## Documentation | Guide | Covers | | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | [Using memory](docs/using-memory.md) | Daily use, capture, recall, memorisations and the user profile | | [Web UI](docs/web-ui.md) | Starting the app, browsing memories and safe network access | | [Memory page](docs/web-ui-memory.md) | One card per host, imports, shared settings and avatars | | [Settings page](docs/web-ui-settings.md) | Models, credentials, diagnostics and profile identities | | [Configuration](docs/configuration.md) | Config files, model selection, privacy and embeddings | | [Moving projects](docs/moving-projects.md) | Folder moves, backup and restore | | [Updating and upgrading](docs/upgrading.md) | Updates, version pinning and older stores | | [CLI reference](docs/cli.md) | Terminal commands | | [Memory spaces](docs/memory-spaces.md) | Separate stores, the Spaces page, backups and the `space` command | | [Skill learning](docs/skill-learning.md) | Opt-in turn recording, skill ranking and draft review | | [For developers](docs/developers.md) | Building, testing and architecture | | [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) | Development workflow and pull requests | History import guides: [OpenCode](docs/opencode-history-import.md), [Pi](docs/pi-history-import.md) and [Claude Code](docs/claude-code-history-import.md).
